claims.statement: The concept applies to FPT, GHEC and GHES. GHES below 3.21 describes conversion of a personal account to an organization; other versions describe moving repositories and projects while preserving the personal account. These are different lifecycle operations.

The legacy conversion passage says repositories are preserved without individual transfers and collaborators are automatically invited to equivalent-permission teams; its following paragraph also says repository collaborators become outside collaborators, optionally invited as members. The relationship between these statements needs reconciliation, not assumed equivalence.

Account deletion removes owned repositories, private-repository forks, wikis, issues, pull requests and Pages. Issues, pull requests and comments in others' repositories remain; cloud versions additionally associate resources and comments with the ghost user. Deletion is not complete erasure of all participation.

In FPT and GHEC deletion stops billing, frees the email address for another account and makes the account name reusable after 90 days. These source effects are not authorization to delete or change billing.

A sole organization owner must transfer ownership or delete the organization before deleting the personal account; where other owners exist, the user must remove themself. Referenced procedures and side effects require separate review and approval.

An email address associates with only one account. After loss of unrecoverable 2FA access, unlinking allows reuse on another account and may reconnect commits using that address; unless email privacy is chosen the commit address matches the primary address.

GitHub-provided noreply addresses cannot be unlinked, and their authored commits cannot be reconnected to another account. Email unlinking does not transfer repositories, permissions or profile from the locked account.

Unlinking is available only for 2FA-enabled accounts; other accounts can sign in and remove an address in settings. Educational benefits cannot transfer through unlinking and require the original applicant account.

Multiple accounts may separate personal open-source and employer-managed identities. The concept says a managed user cannot contribute to public projects and points to enterprise-cloud documentation; this statement is not a universal new permissions grant.

Account switching can retain sessions for multiple identities, including personal and service accounts. Workstation contribution can use mixed protocols or per-repository credentials, but multiple identities increase accidental public disclosure risk.

When a managed user is not required, GitHub recommends one personal identity for personal, open-source and professional work; invitations and membership can span repositories, organizations and enterprises. This is a recommendation, not a mandate to merge identities.

HTTPS versus SSH cloning determines which authentication credentials the workstation uses; the described separation stores credentials for one account for HTTPS and an SSH key for the other. Neither protocol choice alone proves credential isolation or prevents wrong-identity writes.

Linked migration, deletion, recovery, identity-switching, cloning and SSH procedures are unreviewed pointers in this receipt. No lifecycle operation, credential modification or policy acceptance is performed.
